questions.question: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV).

parts.text: What agent is used in the prevention of RSV in some patients? How does it work?
In which patients is it indicated?
Name the two most common non-RSV causes of bronchiolitis in infants and children, with subtypes if appropriate.

parts_raw.text: A.  What agent used in the prevention of RSV in some patients?  How does it work?
In which patients is it indicated?
B.  Name the two most common non-RSV causes of bronchiolitis in infants and children with subtypes if appropriate.

questions.model_answer: a) Palivizumab, a humanized monoclonal antibody directed against a protective epitope on the RSV fusion (F) glycoprotein. It provides passive immunoprophylaxis: given as 15 mg/kg IM monthly (up to 5 doses) beginning ~1 month before the RSV season, it neutralizes RSV and, although it does not prevent infection, it reduces clinical severity, lower respiratory tract disease and hospitalization. b) High-risk infants in the first year of life: (1) prematurity (<29 weeks' gestation); (2) chronic (bronchopulmonary) lung disease; (3) hemodynamically/functionally significant congenital heart disease not surgically corrected; plus chronic conditions that impair handling of respiratory secretions (e.g., neuromuscular disease). In the second year it is reserved for preterm children with chronic lung disease still requiring oxygen/steroids/diuretics. c) (1) Rhinovirus; (2) Human parainfluenza virus (especially type 3); human metapneumovirus is the other frequently cited agent.
questions.beyond_mandell: Mandell lists rhinovirus, adenovirus, coronavirus, parainfluenza, human metapneumovirus and bocavirus as RSV co-infecting viruses but does not rank the leading non-RSV bronchiolitis causes; rhinovirus, parainfluenza type 3 and hMPV are the standard answers.

cohort_answer.text:
Passive immunization with palivizumab – monoclonal immunoglobulin against an epitope on the F glycoprotein of RSV.
Rhinovirus; Parainfluenza type 3; Human metapneumo virus

parts.text: Give the classification of metapneumovirus (Order, Family, Subfamily, Genus, nucleic acid type, envelope).
Describe the clinical presentation and name the risk groups associated with severe disease.

parts_raw.text: A. Give the family/order/genus for metapneumovirus. (Classification, Order, Family, Subfamily, Genus, DNA, Envelope)
B. Describe the clinical presentation and name the risk groups associated with severe disease.

questions.model_answer:
a) Order: Mononegavirales. Family: Pneumoviridae. Subfamily: none (formerly subfamily Pneumovirinae of Paramyxoviridae; reclassified to family Pneumoviridae by ICTV in 2016). Genus: Metapneumovirus. Nucleic acid: single-stranded, negative-sense (nonsegmented) RNA. Envelope: yes, lipid-enveloped, pleomorphic virion with F, G, and SH surface glycoproteins.

b) Presentation: clinical syndrome is not distinct and mirrors RSV, ranging from mild upper respiratory infection to bronchiolitis and severe pneumonia requiring mechanical ventilation; incubation ~5-6 days. Most common symptoms are fever, cough, and coryza. Children: fever (often higher than RSV, with febrile seizures in up to ~16%), cough, sore throat, rhinorrhea, wheezing, and acute otitis media (up to 60% of those <3 yr); hospitalization diagnoses are bronchiolitis (47-84%), asthma/wheezing (11-25%), and pneumonia (11-17%); neurologic complications (seizures, encephalitis) are ~10x more common than with RSV. Adults: healthy adults have mild influenza-like/cold illness; those with cardiopulmonary disease develop severe cough (often without fever) and hospitalization; accounts for 4-12% of COPD, 7% of asthma, and 4% of CAP admissions.
Risk groups for severe disease: (1) young children, especially <2 yr with peak hospitalization at 6-11 months, and prematurity (greatest risk, OR ~14); (2) elderly and adults with chronic cardiopulmonary disease (COPD, CHF, chronic respiratory insufficiency) and long-term care facility residents; (3) immunocompromised hosts, particularly HSCT recipients (LRTI/respiratory failure in ~1/3, mortality up to 80%), solid-organ (including lung) transplant recipients, and patients with hematologic malignancy or on high-dose steroids/lymphopenia.
questions.beyond_mandell: The taxonomic ranks (order Mononegavirales, family Pneumoviridae, ssRNA negative-sense, enveloped) are established from ICTV taxonomy (Rima 2017; Amarasinghe 2017) rather than stated as a table in this chapter slice.

cohort_answer.text:
A: Classification | Metapneumovirus. Order | Mononegavirales. Family | Pneumoviridae. Subfamily | n/a. Genus | Metapneumovirus. DNA | Single-stranded, negative sense RNA. Envelope | Lipid envelope

B (Red Book 32nd edition): Clinical Presentation similar to RSV (hOPV). Incubation period 3-7 days. Spectrum: mild URI to bronchiolitis to severe pneumonia requiring mechanical ventilation. Fever, cough, coryza. In children: febrile seizures, croup, asthma exacerbations, acute otitis media. Bronchiolitis most commonly causes hospitalization at 6-12 months old. Risk factors for severe disease: Children <2 years, Comorbid conditions: Prematurity <32 weeks, underlying heart and lung disease, Immunocompromised (SCT and lung tx recipients)
